messages.content: What is climate change and what is the scientific consensus on its causes?

Climate change refers to long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns. While natural factors have always influenced climate, the scientific consensus — supported by over 97% of actively publishing climate scientists and affirmed by all major scientific organisations globally — is that human activities are the dominant cause of observed warming since the mid-20th century. The mechanism: the greenhouse effect. Solar radiation (primarily visible light) passes through the atmosphere and warms Earth's surface. Earth radiates infrared (heat) radiation back upward. Greenhouse gases (GHGs) — CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, H₂O vapour, ozone, fluorinated gases — absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, warming the atmosphere. This natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth ~33°C warmer than it would otherwise be. Enhanced greenhouse effect: burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) releases CO₂ stored over hundreds of millions of years into the atmosphere in decades. Deforestation (reduces CO₂ uptake). Agriculture (methane from livestock and rice paddies; nitrous oxide from fertilisers). Industrial processes (cement production releases CO₂; fluorinated gases are potent GHGs). Current CO₂ concentration: ~422 ppm (2024) — the highest in at least 800,000 years (from ice cores); pre-industrial level was ~280 ppm. Temperature: global average surface temperature has risen approximately 1.1-1.2°C since pre-industrial times (1850-1900 baseline). Multiple independent lines of evidence: atmospheric CO₂ measurements (Mauna Loa Observatory — Keeling Curve since 1958); ocean heat content; sea level rise; glacier and ice sheet retreat; Arctic sea ice decline; earlier spring timing of biological events; fingerprint studies showing the pattern of warming (stratospheric cooling while troposphere warms — uniquely consistent with greenhouse gas forcing, not solar activity).
What are the effects of climate change and what are the projections?

Climate change is producing wide-ranging and accelerating impacts across natural and human systems. Observed impacts: (1) Temperature: global mean surface temperature rose ~1.1-1.2°C above pre-industrial levels by 2022. Extreme heat events (heatwaves) have increased in frequency, intensity, and duration. The European heatwave (2003): ~70,000 excess deaths. 2023 was the hottest year in recorded history. (2) Sea level rise: ~20 cm since 1900; accelerating; currently ~3.7mm/year. Driven by: thermal expansion of ocean water (accounts for ~40-50% of rise) and melting of glaciers and ice sheets (Greenland ice sheet: ~7m sea level equivalent; West Antarctic Ice Sheet: ~4.8m sea level equivalent — potential tipping point). Small island states (Maldives, Kiribati, Tuvalu) face existential threat. (3) Ocean acidification: oceans absorb ~25% of CO₂ emissions; dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid. Ocean pH has fallen from ~8.2 to ~8.1 (30% increase in acidity). Threatens shell-forming organisms (corals, molluscs, echinoderms) — the base of marine food webs. Coral bleaching (Great Barrier Reef). (4) Extreme weather: attribution science increasingly attributes individual extreme events to climate change. More intense precipitation events (more water vapour in warmer atmosphere); more intense tropical cyclones (warmer oceans provide more energy); longer and more severe droughts (increased evaporation, altered precipitation patterns). (5) Ecosystem disruption: species range shifts poleward and to higher altitude; phenological mismatches (pollinators and flowers no longer synchronised); coral reef collapse at 1.5-2°C. IPCC AR6 projections: without rapid emissions reductions, global warming of 2.5-4.5°C by 2100 is projected under high-emission scenarios, with catastrophic consequences for food security, human displacement, biodiversity, and geopolitical stability.
What are ecosystems and how do they function?

An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (biotic components) interacting with each other and with their non-living physical environment (abiotic components — soil, water, sunlight, temperature, nutrients) in a defined area. Ecosystems can be as small as a tidal pool or as large as the Amazon basin. Structure: producers (autotrophs) capture energy from sunlight (photosynthesis) or chemical reactions (chemosynthesis in deep-sea vents) and produce organic matter — the foundation of the food web. Consumers (heterotrophs): primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary consumers eat herbivores; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi, detritivores) break down dead organic matter, recycling nutrients. Energy flow: energy enters ecosystems primarily through photosynthesis and flows through trophic levels. Only ~10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (the 10% rule) — the rest is lost as heat. This limits the number of trophic levels and explains why food chains are typically short (3-5 levels). The total photosynthetic production is gross primary productivity (GPP); net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP - plant respiration — the energy available to consumers. Nutrient cycling: unlike energy (which flows through and is lost as heat), nutrients are cycled. Biogeochemical cycles: carbon cycle (photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, fossil fuel burning), nitrogen cycle (nitrogen fixation by bacteria, nitrification, denitrification), phosphorus cycle (weathering of rocks, uptake, decomposition — no significant atmospheric reservoir), water cycle. Ecosystem services: provisioning (food, water, timber, medicine), regulating (climate regulation, flood control, water purification, pollination), cultural (recreation, spiritual values), supporting (soil formation, primary production). Ecosystem disturbances: succession — following disturbance (fire, windfall), an ecosystem goes through predictable stages (primary or secondary succession) back toward a climax community.
What is biodiversity and why is it declining?

Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth at all levels — genetic diversity within species, species diversity within ecosystems, and ecosystem diversity across the planet. It represents 3.8 billion years of evolutionary history and is the living fabric of planetary life-support systems. Current status: the world is experiencing its sixth mass extinction event — the first caused by a single species (Homo sapiens). Current extinction rates are estimated at 100-1,000 times background rates; ~1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction (IPBES, 2019). IPBES 2019 Global Assessment: biodiversity is declining faster than at any time in human history; the main drivers (in order of impact): (1) Land-use change: habitat destruction is the dominant driver globally. Agricultural expansion, deforestation, urban expansion, infrastructure. The Amazon basin has lost ~20% of its forest. Tropical forests contain ~50% of terrestrial species on ~7% of land. (2) Direct exploitation: overfishing, hunting, poaching, illegal wildlife trade. Marine fish stocks: one-third are overfished; 60% are fished at maximum sustainable levels. (3) Climate change: increasingly significant; projected to become the dominant driver in the second half of the 21st century. Range shifts, phenological mismatches, coral bleaching. (4) Pollution: nutrient pollution (nitrogen and phosphorus from agriculture causing eutrophication — oxygen depletion in water bodies; dead zones), plastic pollution (8 million tonnes of plastic enters oceans annually; microplastics throughout marine food webs), pesticides (neonicotinoids linked to pollinator decline — global pollinator crisis threatens food security). (5) Invasive species: introduced species outcompete, predate on, or spread disease to native species. Why it matters: biodiversity underpins all ecosystem services — food production, clean water, climate regulation, disease control, and the stability of ecosystems that human civilisation depends on.
What is the nitrogen cycle and why is it important?

The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle through which nitrogen is converted between its various chemical forms as it circulates through atmospheric, terrestrial, and aquatic ecosystems. Nitrogen (N₂) makes up 78% of the atmosphere but is largely inert — most organisms cannot use it directly. Nitrogen fixation converts N₂ to bioavailable forms: biological fixation: nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in legume root nodules — symbiotic fixation; Azotobacter, Cyanobacteria — free-living fixation) use the enzyme nitrogenase to reduce N₂ to NH₃ (ammonia) using 16 ATP molecules. Lightning fixation: lightning provides energy to fix small amounts of atmospheric N₂. Industrial fixation (Haber-Bosch process): N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ using iron catalyst at high temperature (400°C) and pressure (150-300 atm). The Haber-Bosch process fixes approximately as much N per year as all biological fixation — transforming agriculture and enabling it to support ~4 billion people beyond what would have been possible without synthetic fertilisers. Nitrification: ammonia → nitrite (Nitrosomonas) → nitrate (Nitrobacter) — both aerobic processes; makes nitrogen available in forms readily taken up by plant roots. Denitrification: denitrifying bacteria (Pseudomonas) convert nitrate back to N₂ gas in anaerobic conditions — returns nitrogen to the atmosphere. Ammonification: decomposers break down organic matter, releasing ammonia. Human disruption of the nitrogen cycle is one of the most serious planetary boundaries transgressions: reactive nitrogen (Nr) creation has approximately doubled natural fixation rates; excess Nr leads to eutrophication (algal blooms, hypoxic dead zones — Gulf of Mexico dead zone exceeds 20,000 km²), acid deposition, stratospheric ozone depletion (N₂O), ground-level smog, and climate change (N₂O is 265× more potent than CO₂ as a greenhouse gas over 100 years).
What is the Paris Agreement and are countries meeting their targets?

THE PARIS AGREEMENT (2015) — International Climate Framework

WHAT IT IS:
197 countries agreed to limit global warming.
Targets: "well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, pursuing efforts to limit to 1.5°C."
No binding emissions cuts (unlike Kyoto Protocol). Voluntary pledges (NDCs).
NDCs: Nationally Determined Contributions. Each country sets own targets, reviewed every 5 years.
Ambition ratchet: each review should be more ambitious than last.

KEY PROVISIONS:
Climate finance: developed nations pledged $100B/year to developing nations by 2020.
 Missed: reached ~$83B by 2021. Quality disputed.
Loss and damage: new fund for countries suffering climate impacts (agreed COP27, 2022).
Transparency: countries must report emissions, track progress.
Global Stocktake: every 5 years, assess collective progress. First: 2023. Found: far off track.

PROGRESS AS OF 2024:
Current trajectory: ~2.5-3°C by 2100 based on pledges.
Pledges (if fully implemented): ~2.1-2.4°C.
Policies currently in place: ~2.7-3.1°C.
Gap between what''s needed (1.5°C) and what''s happening: enormous.

COUNTRY HIGHLIGHTS:
EU: committed to 55% reduction by 2030 (vs 1990). Generally on track. Carbon market effective.
US: 50-52% reduction by 2030 (vs 2005). IRA (Inflation Reduction Act, 2022): $369B clean energy investment. Progress accelerating.
China: largest emitter. Peak emissions before 2030, net zero by 2060. Coal still expanding in short term.
India: strong renewables growth. Net zero by 2070.
UK: 68% reduction by 2030 (vs 1990). High wind power deployment.

WHAT SCIENTISTS SAY:
1.5°C essentially requires: emissions roughly halve by 2030, net zero by 2050.
Current policies: very far from this. Even 2°C requires rapid acceleration.
Carbon budget: total CO2 we can emit while staying below 1.5°C = ~380 Gt CO2 (as of 2023).
At current rates: budget exhausted in ~9 years.

KEY PROBLEMS:
Oil and gas expansion: many countries including US expanding production.
Fossil fuel subsidies: $7 trillion/year (IMF, including implicit subsidies).
Methane: pledges exist but implementation weak.
Deforestation: Amazon, Congo basin still losing forests.
How does renewable energy work — solar, wind, and storage?

RENEWABLE ENERGY — How the Technologies Work

SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAIC (PV):
Converts light directly to electricity via photoelectric effect.
Silicon solar cell: p-n junction. Photon knocks electron free -> current flows.
Efficiency: commercial panels ~22%. Research cells ~47% (multi-junction concentrator).
Monocrystalline (highest efficiency, most expensive) vs polycrystalline vs thin-film.

Cost: collapsed 99% since 1976. Now cheapest electricity in history.
$0.025/kWh utility solar (2023, best sites). Below cost of any fossil fuel.

Inverter: converts DC from panels to AC for grid. Smart inverters can provide grid stability services.
String inverter: panels in series, one inverter. Shade on one panel affects all.
Microinverter: one per panel. More efficient, more expensive.

WIND:
Horizontal-axis turbines (HAWTs): most common. Blades convert kinetic energy to rotation -> generator.
Offshore wind: stronger, more consistent wind. Larger turbines (15 MW). No noise complaints. More expensive to install/maintain.
Onshore wind: cheapest renewable electricity in windy locations.
Capacity factor: wind turbine produces ~35% of nameplate capacity on average (wind isn''t always blowing).
Modern turbines: 3 blades, variable pitch (angle adjusts for optimal efficiency), yaw (rotates to face wind).

Betz limit: maximum 59.3% of wind kinetic energy can be extracted. Physics limit.
Current best turbines: ~45-50% of Betz limit.

ENERGY STORAGE:
The challenge: sun and wind are variable. Grid needs supply = demand at every instant.

Lithium-ion batteries (grid-scale): 4-hour storage. Tesla Megapack. Prices falling rapidly.
 Best for: smoothing short-term fluctuations, peak demand management.

Pumped hydro: 95% of world''s grid storage capacity. Pump water uphill when cheap energy, release when needed.
 Cheap, long-lived. Requires right geography.

Hydrogen: electrolysis splits water -> H₂. Can store months. Use in fuel cells or combustion.
 Round-trip efficiency: ~30-40%. Expensive. Long-duration storage solution.

Long-duration storage (LDES): iron-air batteries (Form Energy, 100-hour), flow batteries, compressed air.
 Still mostly pre-commercial. Critical for 100% renewable grid.

THE DUCK CURVE:
As solar penetrates, midday demand met by solar. But evening: solar falls, demand spikes.
Grid must ramp up quickly. Batteries are the solution: charge midday, discharge evening.
